```{r}
#| label: preview-data
#| include: false
# Display only: visible code downloads these data later in the deck.
cubes <- cansim::list_cansim_cubes(lite = TRUE)
n_active <- sum(!cubes$archived)

pop_all <- cansim::get_cansim("17-10-0148-01")
n_van_2025 <- sum(pop_all$GEO == "Vancouver (CMA), British Columbia" & pop_all$REF_DATE == "2025")
preview_pop <- pop_all |>
  dplyr::filter(GEO == "Vancouver (CMA), British Columbia", REF_DATE == "2025",
                Gender %in% c("Total - gender", "Men+"),
                `Age group` %in% c("All ages", "0 to 4 years", "Average age")) |>
  dplyr::relocate(REF_DATE, GEO, Gender, `Age group`, VALUE, UOM)
rm(pop_all)

census_2021 <- cancensus::get_census("CA21", regions = list(CMA = "59933"),
                                     level = "CMA", quiet = TRUE)$Population

cmhc_all <- cmhc::get_cmhc("Rms", "Vacancy Rate", "Bedroom Type",
                           "Historical Time Periods", geo_uid = "59933")
preview_cmhc <- cmhc_all |> dplyr::filter(Date == max(Date))

# StatCan's republished vacancy rate against CMHC's own headline rate
vac_compare <- cansim::get_cansim("34-10-0127-01") |>
  dplyr::filter(GEO == "Vancouver, British Columbia") |>
  dplyr::transmute(year = lubridate::year(Date), statcan = VALUE) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    cmhc_all |>
      dplyr::filter(`Bedroom Type` == "Total") |>
      dplyr::transmute(year = lubridate::year(Date), cmhc = Value),
    by = "year"
  )
n_vac_differ <- sum(vac_compare$statcan != vac_compare$cmhc)
```

## StatCan or CMHC?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Statistics Canada

About `r format(round(n_active, -2), big.mark = ",")` active data tables on every subject: prices, population, income, and construction.

Mostly for Canada, provinces, and CMAs; monthly or annual.

Use it for long series and broad topics.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### CMHC

Housing only, in more detail: the rental market, housing starts and completions, condo rentals, and seniors' housing.

Down to neighbourhoods and census tracts.

Use it for rental and construction detail in small areas.
:::
::::

StatCan republishes a few CMHC series, with less detail.

::: {.notes}
- StatCan: [statcan.gc.ca](https://www.statcan.gc.ca/en/start). `cansim::search_cansim_cubes("vacancy")` searches the table titles from R.
- CMHC: the [Housing Market Information Portal](https://www03.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/hmip-pimh/en) shows every CMHC table and downloads it as a CSV. The `cmhc` package reads the same tables.
- Neither needs an API key.
:::

## Tables for real estate

::: {.small}
| Table | What it measures | Places | Since |
|---|---|---|---|
| [17-10-0148-01](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1710014801) | Population estimates, July 1, by age and gender | CMAs | 2001, annual |
| [18-10-0005-01](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1810000501) | Consumer Price Index, annual average | Canada, provinces, 19 cities | 1914, annual |
| [18-10-0004-01](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1810000401) | Consumer Price Index | Canada, provinces, 19 cities | 1914, monthly |
| [18-10-0205-01](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1810020501) | New housing price index: total, house, and land | Canada, provinces, CMAs | 1981, monthly |
| [34-10-0292-01](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=3410029201) | Building permits: number, units, and value | Canada, provinces, CMAs | 2018, monthly |
| [34-10-0156-01](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=3410015601) | CMHC housing starts, by type of unit | Canada, provinces, CMAs | 1990, monthly |
| [34-10-0127-01](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=3410012701) | CMHC vacancy rates | CMAs | 1971, annual |
| [34-10-0133-01](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=3410013301) | CMHC average rents, by unit type | Centres of 10,000+ | 1987, annual |
| [34-10-0145-01](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=3410014501) | CMHC 5-year mortgage rate | Canada | 1951, monthly |
:::

The table number is what you give `get_cansim()`, or your agent.

::: {.notes}
- "Since" is the first year in the table. Many places start later: the Vancouver CPI, for example, does not go back to 1914.
- The CPI's 19 cities include Vancouver, Victoria, Calgary, Edmonton, Toronto, and Montréal.
- The research project page lists these and other sources.
:::

## A StatCan table: one row per date, place, and category

```{r}
#| label: preview-statcan
#| echo: false
#| classes: data-preview
preview_table(preview_pop)
```

Six of the `r n_van_2025` rows for Vancouver CMA in 2025. Each row is one gender and one age group. `UOM` says whether `VALUE` counts persons or years.

::: {.notes}
- Gender and Age group are the table's dimensions. Every StatCan table has `Date`, `GEO`, `VALUE`, `UOM`, and `SCALAR_FACTOR`, plus its own dimensions.
- "Total - gender" is the sum of Men+ and Women+, and "All ages" is the sum of the age groups. The table holds totals and their parts in the same column.
:::

## A CMHC table: one row per date and category

```{r}
#| label: preview-cmhc
#| echo: false
#| classes: data-preview
preview_table(preview_cmhc)
```

Vacancy rates in the Vancouver CMA, October `r lubridate::year(max(cmhc_all$Date))`. `Quality` rates each value, from Excellent to "Fair (Use with Caution)". CMHC withholds values too unreliable to publish: they come back as `NA`.

## What each source counts

::: {.small}
| Data | Counts | Watch for |
|---|---|---|
| Population estimates | People on July 1, on 2021 boundaries for every year | Estimates, not census counts: the 2021 Census counted `r format(census_2021, big.mark = ",")` |
| CPI | Prices of a fixed basket of goods, 2002 = 100 | Not seasonally adjusted |
| StatCan housing starts | Units started, seasonally adjusted at **annual rates** | Each month is a yearly pace: do not add months |
| CMHC Rental Market Survey | Purpose-built rentals in buildings of 3+ units, each October | Leaves out rented condos and basement suites |
| StatCan vacancy rates | Apartments in buildings of 6+ units | Differs from CMHC's headline rate in `r n_vac_differ` of `r nrow(vac_compare)` years |
:::

::: {.key-point}
An agent can find a table. Whether the table counts what your question needs is your call.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Population estimates add births, deaths, and migration to the last census and adjust for people the census missed, so the 2021 estimate is higher than the census count.
- The rental survey and StatCan's vacancy table differ by 0.1 to 0.2 points in those years, because they count different buildings.
- CMHC's own Starts and Completions Survey (`survey = "Scss"` in the `cmhc` package) gives monthly counts that can be added up.
:::

## Quick check: which source and table?

Where would you look for:

1. Two-bedroom rents in Kitsilano and in Marpole since 2015?
2. Whether Vancouver's population growth is slowing?
3. Whether new-home prices have kept up with inflation?
4. How many homes were started in the Vancouver CMA each year?

::: {.fragment .small}
1. CMHC's Rental Market Survey, by survey zone: "Kitsilano/Point Grey" and "Marpole". StatCan stops at the CMA.
2. StatCan 17-10-0148-01.
3. StatCan's new housing price index, 18-10-0205-01, against the CPI, 18-10-0005-01.
4. CMHC's Starts and Completions Survey. StatCan's 34-10-0156-01 gives annual rates, which do not add up to a year.
:::

# A StatCan table with an agent

## We asked an agent

::: {.small}
```text
Plot the population of the Vancouver CMA from 2001 to 2025 using
Statistics Canada data. Download it with cansim.
```
:::

It had to choose a table, and said why:

> StatCan has two CMA population tables. `17-10-0135-01` (2016 boundaries) ends at 2022, so it can't cover your period; I used `17-10-0148-01` (2021 boundaries, 2001–2025).

It also noted that these are estimates, not census counts.

::: {.notes}
- Tested on 2026-11-06 with Claude Code (Opus 5) in two fresh copies of the student `c407` folder. The prompt is exactly as shown.
- Neither run asked a question: the period settled the choice of table. Both chose 17-10-0148-01 and the same filters. Run 1 filtered on the code `GeoUID == "933"` instead of the place name.
- StatCan's site was down during the test; run 2 waited about 10 minutes and tried again. Downloads can fail for a while: try again later.
:::

## The agent's code

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: packages
library(tidyverse)
library(cansim)
```

```{r}
#| label: agent-population
#| output: false
# Table 17-10-0148-01: population estimates as of 1 July, by CMA and CA, on
# 2021 census boundaries. The older 17-10-0135-01 (2016 boundaries) stops at
# 2022, so it cannot cover the requested period.
cma_pop_raw <- get_cansim("17-10-0148-01")

van_pop <- cma_pop_raw |>
  # "All ages" drops the single-year and average/median-age rows; "Total -
  # gender" avoids double counting Men+ and Women+. Together these leave one
  # headcount per year.
  filter(
    GEO == "Vancouver (CMA), British Columbia",
    `Age group` == "All ages",
    Gender == "Total - gender",
    REF_DATE >= "2001", REF_DATE <= "2025"
  ) |>
  transmute(year = as.integer(REF_DATE), population = val_norm) |>
  arrange(year)

glimpse(van_pop)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
- `get_cansim()` downloads the whole table: every place, gender, age group, and year, about `r round(nrow(cma_pop_raw) / 1e6, 1)` million rows.
- `transmute()` keeps only the columns it creates.
:::

## Your prompt became three filters

::: {.small}
| Your prompt | The agent's code |
|---|---|
| "the Vancouver CMA" | `GEO == "Vancouver (CMA), British Columbia"` |
| "from 2001 to 2025" | `REF_DATE >= "2001", REF_DATE <= "2025"` |
| "population" | Table 17-10-0148-01, `` `Age group` == "All ages" ``, and `Gender == "Total - gender"` |
:::

"Population" became a table and two filters you did not write.

The agent also used `val_norm`, not `VALUE`. It turns percentages into proportions, so 5% becomes 0.05. Here the two are the same.

::: {.key-point}
Every dimension of a StatCan table needs a filter. Each filter the agent chose is a decision: read them all.
:::

## Check: one row per year

```{r}
#| label: one-row
van_pop |> count(year) |> distinct(n)
```

`count(year)` should show exactly one row per year before you plot or sum.

## What the filters removed

```{r}
#| label: dims
cma_pop_raw |>
  filter(GEO == "Vancouver (CMA), British Columbia", REF_DATE == "2025") |>
  count(Gender, UOM)
```

::: {.warning}
Without the filters, summing `VALUE` counts each person several times and adds ages in years to people. R will not stop you.
:::

## Vancouver's population over time

```{r}
#| label: pop-plot
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The agent's chart code"
van_pop |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = population)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2001, 2025, 4)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Population",
    caption = "Statistics Canada, table 17-10-0148-01 (2021 CMA boundaries)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.notes}
- `label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")` writes 3,000,000 as 3M. Deck 12 covers scales.
- Both runs noted the slowdown in 2025 and linked it to the caps on temporary residents, and both said the table cannot show the cause.
:::

## Quick check: which filters change?

You now want **Calgary's population aged 65 and older, by gender**, from 2001 to 2025.

Which lines of the agent's `filter()` change? How many rows per year should the check find?

::: {.fragment}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: calgary
#| eval: false
filter(
  GEO == "Calgary (CMA), Alberta",
  `Age group` == "65 years and older",
  Gender != "Total - gender",
  REF_DATE >= "2001", REF_DATE <= "2025"
)
```
:::

Three of the four. "By gender" keeps Men+ and Women+ and drops their total, so the check should find two rows per year.
:::

# Real prices with an agent

## We asked an agent to adjust for inflation

::: {.small}
```text
Using data/bca262.rds, plot the median sale price by year from 2000
to 2025, adjusted for inflation. Get the CPI from Statistics Canada
with cansim.
```
:::

Before plotting, it asked whether to pool the two property types:

::: {.small}
| Option | Change in real prices, 2000 to 2025 |
|---|---|
| **1. One line per property type** | Single-family +259%, strata +158% |
| **2. One pooled line** | +113% |
| **3. Both** | The pooled line beside the two types |
:::

Strata units were 45% of sales in 2000 and 76% in 2025, so the pooled median partly tracks which homes sold. This is the mix shift from deck 05. We chose 1.

::: {.notes}
- Tested on 2026-11-06 with Claude Code (Opus 5) in two fresh copies of the student `c407` folder. The prompt is exactly as shown.
- Both runs asked this question, with the same numbers, and recommended option 1. We answered "1".
- Ask the class why the agent could not decide this for us: both lines are correct; they answer different questions.
:::

## The agent's code: sales and CPI

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: agent-cpi
bca <- read_rds("data/bca262.rds")

# Sales stop on 11 March 2026, so 2026 is a partial year and is left out.
sales <- bca |>
  mutate(year = year(sale_date)) |>
  filter(year %in% 2000:2025)

# Table 18-10-0005 is the annual-average CPI. Annual averages line up with
# annual medians, so no monthly aggregation is needed. Vancouver CMA is used
# rather than Canada so that local inflation does the deflating.
cpi_raw <- get_cansim("18-10-0005")

cpi_van <- cpi_raw |>
  filter(`Products and product groups` == "All-items",
         GEO == "Vancouver, British Columbia") |>
  transmute(year = as.integer(REF_DATE), cpi = VALUE) |>
  filter(year %in% 2000:2025)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Run 2's code, shortened: the `cat()` lines that print row counts are left out.
:::

## The agent's code: real medians

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: agent-real
# 2025 is the base year, so every price is expressed in 2025 dollars.
cpi_base <- cpi_van |> filter(year == 2025) |> pull(cpi)

median_nominal_by_year <- sales |>
  summarise(.by = c(year, act_use_cat),
            n_sales = n(),
            median_nominal = median(price))

# relationship = "many-to-one": many year-by-type rows match one CPI row per
# year, and a duplicated CPI year would stop with an error instead of silently
# duplicating sales rows.
median_by_year <- median_nominal_by_year |>
  left_join(cpi_van, by = "year", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  # Every sale in a year shares one deflator, so deflating the median gives the
  # same answer as deflating each sale and then taking the median.
  mutate(median_real = median_nominal * cpi_base / cpi,
         property_type = if_else(act_use_cat == "S/F Res",
                                 "Single-family",
                                 "Strata (condo or townhouse)"))
```
:::

`median_real` is the price × (CPI in 2025 ÷ CPI in the year of sale).

## Three choices it did not ask about

::: {.small}
| Choice | The agent's pick | Other options |
|---|---|---|
| Table | 18-10-0005-01, annual averages | 18-10-0004-01, monthly |
| Place | Vancouver | British Columbia, Canada |
| Dollars | 2025 dollars | Any other year |
:::

It said none of these changes the shape of the line. Check the place:

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: cpi-places
cpi_raw |>
  filter(`Products and product groups` == "All-items", REF_DATE %in% c("2000", "2025"),
         GEO %in% c("Canada", "British Columbia", "Vancouver, British Columbia")) |>
  select(GEO, REF_DATE, VALUE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = REF_DATE, values_from = VALUE)
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: cpi-numbers
#| include: false
cpi_growth <- cpi_raw |>
  filter(`Products and product groups` == "All-items", REF_DATE %in% c("2000", "2025"),
         GEO %in% c("Canada", "British Columbia", "Vancouver, British Columbia")) |>
  summarise(growth = VALUE[REF_DATE == "2025"] / VALUE[REF_DATE == "2000"], .by = GEO) |>
  deframe()
```

## The choice it asked about mattered more

From 2000 to 2025, prices rose `r round(cpi_growth[["Vancouver, British Columbia"]], 2)`-fold in Vancouver and `r round(cpi_growth[["Canada"]], 2)`-fold in Canada. Switching the CPI moves every real price by about `r round(100 * (cpi_growth[["Canada"]] / cpi_growth[["Vancouver, British Columbia"]] - 1))`%.

Pooling the property types moved the answer from +259% to +113%.

::: {.key-point}
The agent asked about the choice that changed the answer. Check the ones it did not ask about anyway: each takes a few lines.
:::

## Check the arithmetic

```{r}
#| label: check-2000
median_by_year |>
  filter(year == 2000) |>
  select(property_type, median_nominal, cpi, median_real)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-numbers
#| include: false
sf_2000 <- median_by_year |> filter(year == 2000, act_use_cat == "S/F Res")
```

By hand, for single-family homes: `r scales::comma(sf_2000$median_nominal)` × `r cpi_base` ÷ `r sf_2000$cpi` = `r scales::comma(sf_2000$median_real)`. A median from 2000 in 2025 dollars.

## Real prices by property type

```{r}
#| label: real-plot
#| fig-height: 3
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Chart code"
ggplot(median_by_year, aes(year, median_real, colour = property_type)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Median sale price, 2025 dollars", colour = NULL,
       caption = "Sources: BC Assessment; Statistics Canada Table 18-10-0005-01")
```

```{r}
#| label: real-numbers
#| include: false
sf <- median_by_year |> filter(act_use_cat == "S/F Res")
fold <- function(x) round(x[sf$year == 2025] / x[sf$year == 2000], 1)
```

::: {.warning}
From 2000 to 2025 the single-family median rose `r fold(sf$median_nominal)`-fold in nominal dollars, but `r fold(sf$median_real)`-fold in 2025 dollars. Say which dollars every axis uses.
:::

# CMHC data with an agent

## We asked an agent

::: {.small}
```text
Using the cmhc package, plot rental vacancy rates by bedroom type
in the Vancouver CMA since 1990.
```
:::

It asked nothing. Both runs downloaded the same `r nrow(cmhc_all)` values: 36 Octobers × 5 bedroom categories, the four types and their total.

Both noticed that the course file `data/cmhc_vacancy_vancouver.csv` holds the same series, and one run checked that the 1990 values match.

::: {.notes}
- Tested on 2026-11-06 with Claude Code (Opus 5) in two fresh copies of the student `c407` folder. The prompt is exactly as shown.
- Run 2 called `get_cmhc()` without `filters` and got the same values.
- No API key is needed, but the download needs CMHC's site to be up.
:::

## The agent's code

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: agent-cmhc
library(cmhc)

# geo_uid 59933 is the Vancouver CMA (see cmhc_cma_translation_data).
# "Row / Apartment" is CMHC's full purpose-built rental universe and the basis
# of its headline published vacancy rate; the October survey is the only one
# that reaches back to 1990 (April runs only 2007-2015).
vacancy <- get_cmhc(
  survey = "Rms",
  series = "Vacancy Rate",
  dimension = "Bedroom Type",
  breakdown = "Historical Time Periods",
  geo_uid = "59933",
  filters = list(dwelling_type_desc_en = "Row / Apartment", season = "October")
)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Run 1's code. `glimpse(vacancy)` after it is left out.
:::

## Your prompt set five arguments

::: {.small}
| Your prompt | Argument |
|---|---|
| "rental vacancy rates" | `survey = "Rms"`, `series = "Vacancy Rate"` |
| "by bedroom type" | `dimension = "Bedroom Type"` |
| "since 1990" | `breakdown = "Historical Time Periods"`: years for one place |
| "the Vancouver CMA" | `geo_uid = "59933"` |
:::

The agent added `filters`, which you did not ask for. These two match the defaults, so the numbers do not change. `season = "April"` would: April surveys ran only from 2007 to 2015.

::: {.notes}
- `breakdown = "Survey Zones"` returns places for one year instead, as on the next slide.
- `list_cmhc_surveys()`, `list_cmhc_series()`, `list_cmhc_dimensions()`, and `list_cmhc_breakdowns()` list the other choices.
- `59933` is the census code for the Vancouver CMA, the same as in `get_census()`.
:::

## Check the quality codes

```{r}
#| label: quality-cma
count(vacancy, Quality)
```

For the whole CMA, every value is Good or better.

::: {.notes}
The package labels code d "Fair (Use with Caution)"; the note in CMHC's CSV calls it "Poor (Use with Caution)".
:::

## Small areas have weaker values

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: quality-zones
rents_zone <- get_cmhc(survey = "Rms", series = "Average Rent",
                       dimension = "Bedroom Type", breakdown = "Survey Zones",
                       geo_uid = "59933", year = 2025)
count(rents_zone, Quality)
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: quality-numbers
#| include: false
n_weak <- sum(is.na(rents_zone$Quality) | rents_zone$Quality == "Fair (Use with Caution)")
```

Average rents by survey zone in 2025: `r n_weak` of `r nrow(rents_zone)` are "Fair (Use with Caution)" or withheld.

::: {.warning}
The smaller the area, the fewer units CMHC surveys. Check `Quality` before you compare areas.
:::

## What "rental" left out

The Rental Market Survey counts purpose-built rentals in buildings of 3+ units, each October. Condos rented out by their owners are in a different survey:

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: srms
list_cmhc_series("Srms")
```
:::

One run told us its series leaves out condo rentals; the other did not. If your question is about everyone who rents, the survey you need may not be the one the agent picked.

## Practice: read CMHC's own download

The portal also downloads tables as CSV files, such as `data/cmhc_vacancy_vancouver.csv`. Ask your agent:

::: {.small}
```text
Read data/cmhc_vacancy_vancouver.csv and plot vacancy rates by
bedroom type.
```
:::

Before you trust the chart:

1. How many rows did it keep? The file covers 1990 to 2025.
2. Are the rates numbers, not text?
3. What did it do with the letters after each rate?

::: {.notes}
The prompt is untested with an agent.
:::

## Answer: the file

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: cmhc-raw
read_lines("data/cmhc_vacancy_vancouver.csv", skip = 2, n_max = 3)
```
:::

- One column per bedroom type: the table is wide.
- After each rate comes a column with no name. It holds a reliability code, from a (excellent) to d (poor: use with caution).
- Two title lines sit above the table, and notes below it.

## Answer: the code

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: cmhc-read
vacancy_w <- read_csv("data/cmhc_vacancy_vancouver.csv", skip = 2, n_max = 36) |>
  select(year = 1, Studio, `1 Bedroom`, `2 Bedroom`, `3 Bedroom +`, Total) |>
  mutate(year = parse_number(year))
vacancy_w |> head(3)
```
:::

- 36 rows. Without `n_max = 36`, CMHC's notes become five more rows, and `Studio` turns into text.
- `select()` keeps the rates and drops the code columns.

::: {.notes}
- `read_csv()` names the columns without a name `...1`, `...3`, and so on, and says so in a message. `select(year = 1)` keeps the first column and names it `year`.
- The file is in Windows-1252, not UTF-8: the dash in its first line prints as `\x97`. Skipping the title lines avoids it.
- Rent tables are harder: rents are text with commas, such as "1,684", and suppressed cells are `**`.
- To plot one line per bedroom type, make the table long with `pivot_longer()`, as in deck 07.
:::

## What to know from this deck

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
**Know**<br>*Write it without help*

::: {.small}
- StatCan for long series; CMHC for rental detail
- `get_cansim("table number")`
- `count(Date) |> distinct(n)`
- price × CPI₂₀₂₅ ÷ CPI
- `count(x, Quality)`
:::
:::

::: {.column width="32%"}
**Recognize**<br>*Say what the line does*

::: {.small}
- `VALUE`, `UOM`, `val_norm`
- `get_cmhc()`: survey, series, dimension, breakdown, geo_uid
- `filters =` in `get_cmhc()`
- "at annual rates"
- `Rms` and `Srms`
:::
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
**Look up**<br>*When you meet it*

- `search_cansim_cubes()`
- `list_cmhc_series()`
- `list_cmhc_breakdowns()`
- CMHC's Housing Market Information Portal
:::
